strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across four diverse MoE models (Mixtral-8x7B, DeepSeek-MoE-16B, Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, Qwen3-MoE-30B-A3B) and seven general benchmarks plus math reasoning tasks (GSM8K, Math-500, AIME24/25), consistently showing PuzzleMoE preserves accuracy far better than prior expert-dropping/merging baselines (NAEE, STUN, D2, HC-SMoE, Sub-MoE) at 25% and 50% sparsity.

The dual-mask (similarity + saliency) formulation is intuitive and well-motivated, and the authors provide a theoretical derivation (Appendix B.2) explaining why entry-wise weight similarity arises across experts under a normal-weight-distribution assumption, with empirical validation against three of the four models.

The bit-packing scheme that repurposes underused exponent bits in Bfloat16 to store masks/signs without extra memory is a clever systems contribution, backed by a custom CUDA decode kernel and demonstrated to incur no perplexity loss from the shift/pack transformation (Table 1).

Thorough ablations covering calibration dataset choice, number of experts merged, grouping strategy (random vs. search-based), similarity threshold sensitivity, importance-scoring function choice, and compatibility with quantization, plus 16-seed robustness studies with reported means/stds.

Efficiency analysis is convincing: large reductions in offline compression time (2–10 minutes vs. tens of minutes or intractable exhaustive search for NAEE) and demonstrated GPU-count reduction for inference deployment, alongside measured speedups.

Notably strong preservation of reasoning capability under compression (e.g., retaining ~84–99% of baseline accuracy on Math-500/AIME) compared to catastrophic collapse of HC-SMoE, which is a meaningful practical result given the difficulty of preserving reasoning under compression.
weaknesses: The pairwise merging design fundamentally caps compression at 50% (halving expert count); the paper shows that extending to 3-expert groups both hurts accuracy and breaks the bit-packing scheme (insufficient free bits), limiting the method's flexibility relative to approaches offering a continuum of compression ratios.

The exponent-shift bit-packing procedure clips/rounds exponents below 112 and only allocates a 5-bit range; it is unclear how weights with exponents above the observed range (outliers) are handled, and only a single perplexity comparison (Table 1) is used to justify "no degradation," which may not capture rarer failure cases or accumulated error across layers.

Reported inference speedups (1.19–1.28×) are relatively modest given the 50% parameter reduction, and the GEMV kernel description strongly suggests optimization for decode (batch-size-1) settings; the paper does not clearly address how prefill (matrix-matrix) computation handles the packed/masked format or whether overhead from on-the-fly decoding is fully amortized in that regime.

Baseline comparisons partially rely on numbers copied from other papers with differing sparsity levels (e.g., D2 evaluated at 20%/40% instead of 25%/50%) and incomplete metrics (missing entries in Sub-MoE rows), which weakens the strict comparability of the accuracy tables despite the authors' acknowledgment of this discrepancy.

Some large baseline degradations (e.g., HC-SMoE perplexity exploding to 78–175 at 50% sparsity) seem unusually severe compared to typical literature reports, raising a question of whether baseline reproduction settings (e.g., calibration, hyperparameters) were tuned as carefully as PuzzleMoE's, which could inflate the apparent margin of improvement.

The random and search-based expert grouping strategies are described only briefly (e.g., "evolutionary search-based grouping") without full algorithmic detail, and it is unclear whether pairing is consistent across layers or independently randomized per layer, limiting reproducibility of this component.

The core techniques build closely on established ideas (Wanda-style activation-weighted saliency, sparse task-arithmetic merging as in Localize-and-Stitch, exponent-bit reuse observed in prior storage-compressibility work), so novelty lies primarily in combining these ideas for MoE experts rather than introducing fundamentally new mechanisms.
No public code link is provided in the manuscript (placeholder appears empty), so full reproducibility depends on future code release that cannot be verified at review time.

strengths: The dual-mask (similarity + saliency) entry-wise merging is a reasonably novel idea for MoE compression that is more fine-grained than prior coarse expert-level clustering/SVD merging approaches, and the paper provides a plausible theoretical justification (Appendix B.2) for why entry-wise weight similarity exists across experts.

Extensive empirical evaluation across four MoE models (Mixtral-8x7B, DeepSeek-MoE, Qwen1.5-MoE, Qwen3-MoE) and seven benchmarks, plus math reasoning tasks (GSM8K, Math-500, AIME), showing PuzzleMoE retains accuracy substantially better than baselines (NAEE, STUN, D2, HC-SMoE, Sub-MoE) at 25% and 50% expert sparsity.

The bit-packing scheme that embeds masks/signs into underused exponent bits of bfloat16 is a practical systems contribution, supported by a custom CUDA kernel and measured end-to-end memory/latency benefits (single-GPU deployment, up to 1.28x speedup).

Reasonably thorough ablations: calibration dataset choice, number of experts merged, expert grouping strategy (random vs. search), similarity threshold, and importance scoring function, with multiple random seeds reported to demonstrate robustness of the random pairwise grouping choice.
Compression time is shown to be dramatically lower than SVD-based (D2) or exhaustive-search (NAEE) methods, which is a meaningful practical advantage for scalability to models with many experts.
weaknesses: The quantization-compatibility experiment (Table 10) actually undermines the paper's core value proposition: for Mixtral-8x7B, plain AWQ at a lower average bitwidth (3.25 vs 3.35) achieves both better perplexity (4.41 vs 4.50) and better accuracy (73.0 vs 72.4) than PuzzleMoE+quantization, with no expert merging at all. This suggests the proposed sparse merging offers little or even negative value once quantization is applied, which is the realistic deployment setting, but the text does not acknowledge this contradiction and instead frames the result positively.

The method is fundamentally restricted to pairwise expert merging; the ablation on merging 3 experts shows clear degradation and is described as 'impractical' due to bit-width limits. This caps the achievable compression ratio at effectively 50% (merging pairs into one), limiting the generality and future scalability of the approach despite the title's claim of general 'efficient compression.'

Several baseline numbers in the main comparison table (Table 2) are reported with missing entries ("-") and appear to be copied directly from other papers' reported settings rather than reproduced under identical experimental conditions, raising concerns about the fairness and comparability of the headline accuracy gains.

The measured inference speedups (1.19x–1.28x) are fairly modest relative to the architectural/systems effort invested (custom CUDA kernel, bit-packing, on-the-fly decoding), and the evaluation is limited to a GEMV kernel setting without discussion of batched/multi-request serving scenarios that are standard in real deployment.

The core techniques are largely a recombination of existing ideas (Wanda-style magnitude×activation saliency, exponent-bit reuse already explored in cited prior work such as Su et al. 2024 and Zhang et al. 2025, percent-difference similarity), with originality concentrated mainly in combining them for MoE expert merging rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: no working code link is provided in the abstract/manuscript body, and some implementation details (e.g., exact CUDA kernel scheduling, handling of edge cases in sign/mask packing for all MoE architectures) are not fully specified in the main text.

While the paper claims a 'task-agnostic design' as a key differentiator (Figure 1b), the method still relies on a calibration dataset (C4) for saliency computation, and robustness to calibration choice is only demonstrated on a single model (Mixtral-8x7B) rather than across all four evaluated models.

strengths: The dual-mask design (similarity-based mask for shared knowledge + saliency-based mask for specialization) is a well-motivated and intuitively clean solution to the identified tension between shared and expert-specific knowledge in MoE compression, and is validated with a probabilistic analysis in Appendix B.2 explaining why element-wise similarity exists across expert weights.

The bit-packing scheme that reuses underutilized exponent bits in Bfloat16 to embed masks/signs without extra metadata storage is a nice systems contribution; the accompanying custom GEMV CUDA kernel and empirical confirmation of zero perplexity degradation after the exponent shift (Table 1) make the efficiency claims credible.

Extensive empirical evaluation across four MoE architectures (Mixtral-8x7B, DeepSeek-MoE, Qwen1.5-MoE, Qwen3-MoE) and seven general benchmarks plus domain-specific math/reasoning tasks (GSM8K, Math-500, AIME24/25), showing consistently small accuracy drops even at 50% sparsity, in contrast to the severe degradation of baselines like HC-SMoE and Sub-MoE.

Strong efficiency results: ~45x faster compression than D2, substantial memory reduction enabling single-GPU deployment of models that otherwise require two GPUs, and measurable inference speedups (1.28x / 1.19x).

Thorough ablation studies (calibration dataset choice, number of experts merged, expert grouping strategy, similarity threshold sweep, importance scoring function, compatibility with quantization) and reporting of variance across 16 random seeds, which strengthens confidence in the robustness of the method and reduces concerns about cherry-picked configurations.
weaknesses: The method is fundamentally limited to pairwise merging; the ablation (Table 6) shows that merging 3 experts degrades perplexity and that the bit-packing scheme becomes infeasible beyond pairwise merges (mask+sign encoding exceeds the 3 redundant exponent bits), so the approach cannot be extended to compression ratios beyond 50% without a different storage mechanism, limiting generality.

Baseline numbers for several competitors (STUN, D2, Sub-MoE) are reported with missing entries ("-") in multiple columns, suggesting these are taken directly from the original papers rather than being independently reproduced under this work's exact settings; this raises some concern about strict apples-to-apples comparability, particularly regarding calibration data and evaluation harness consistency.

The custom CUDA kernel is described specifically as a GEMV kernel, and the efficiency evaluation focuses on single-GPU decode-style measurements; it's unclear how the approach performs for batched/prefill-heavy inference scenarios common in production MoE serving, where GEMM rather than GEMV dominates.

The random pairwise grouping strategy is shown to perform nearly as well as a search-based strategy (Table 7), which is good for simplicity but somewhat weakens the paper's narrative that careful, principled expert pairing matters — the gains appear to come almost entirely from the per-entry masking rather than pairing choice, and this could be discussed more critically.

While the paper is described as training-free, it still relies on activation statistics from calibration data to compute saliency masks; although shown to be robust across C4 vs Math corpora, the framing as fully "task-agnostic" could be nuanced further given this dependency on forward-pass activation calibration.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated fine-grained, element-wise expert merging strategy (dual-mask: similarity + activation-weight saliency) that moves beyond coarse-grained expert dropping/clustering/low-rank merging, addressing the well-documented failure mode of prior methods (large accuracy drops at high compression).

Provides a theoretical justification (Lemma 3.1, derived under a Gaussian/independence assumption) for element-wise weight similarity across experts, and validates it empirically against real MoE weight distributions (Figure 2, Appendix A.5/A.6), lending some principled grounding to the approach.

The bit-packing scheme that reuses underutilized BFloat16 exponent bits to embed masks and signs is a clever systems contribution that avoids the metadata overhead that typically negates fine-grained sparsity gains; this is paired with a custom decode-GEMM Triton kernel showing consistent ~2x kernel-level speedup and up to 1.80x end-to-end throughput gains, backed by kernel benchmarks on two GPU architectures (Appendix A.1, A.2).

Extensive empirical evaluation: 4 MoE models, 9 benchmarks (general + math + coding), multiple compression ratios, 16 random seeds for variance analysis, ablations on calibration data, similarity threshold, saliency metric variants, expert grouping strategy, and compatibility with quantization — this is a thorough and largely reproducible experimental protocol with algorithmic details (Algorithm 1) and hyperparameters (τsim, calibration set size) explicitly reported.

Results show substantial and consistent improvements over multiple strong baselines (HC-SMoE, D2, Sub-MoE, NAEE, STUN, Wanda 2:4) especially at high sparsity (50%, and extended to 66.7%/75% in appendix), with dramatic gaps in some domain-specific/reasoning settings (e.g., HC-SMoE collapsing to near-zero accuracy on AIME/HumanEval while PuzzleMoE retains most performance).
weaknesses: The efficient bit-packed inference scheme is inherently tied to pairwise (2-to-1) merging; the paper acknowledges (A.8.4) that higher-ratio merging without explicit mask storage is not directly supported by the packing scheme, which somewhat limits the generality of the efficient-inference contribution beyond 50% sparsity granularity.

The definitions and mechanics of achieving 25% (vs. 50%) sparsity via pairwise merging are not clearly explained in the main text — it is unclear how partial expert reduction is realized when the core operation merges pairs into one, which could confuse reproducibility of that specific setting.

The theoretical model (Lemma 3.1) assumes independent Gaussian weight elements across experts, but the paper's own analysis (Table 7) shows non-negligible correlation (0.26) for Mixtral-8x7B, one of the four evaluated models, somewhat undercutting the generality of the theoretical justification even though empirical curves still roughly track predictions.

Several baseline numbers in Table 1 are directly taken from prior papers with dashes for missing metrics/settings (e.g., D2, Sub-MoE rows), raising potential concerns about exact comparability of evaluation protocols (e.g., differing calibration set, exact sparsity level such as 20% vs 25%) across methods.

The saliency mask still relies on calibration activations (input samples), meaning the method is not entirely training/calibration-free as implied by some framing, though robustness to calibration choice is demonstrated (Table 4).

The throughput evaluation section focuses on comparison against the uncompressed baseline only; a more complete efficiency picture would benefit from comparing decode-GEMM throughput/memory against other compression baselines (e.g., a quantized or CSR-sparse baseline) rather than only cuBLAS dense GEMM.

strengths: The core idea of fine-grained, element-wise dual-mask merging (similarity mask for redundant elements + saliency mask for specialized elements) is a sensible and reasonably novel extension beyond coarse expert-/tensor-level merging used in prior work (HC-SMoE, D2, Sub-MoE).

The bit-packing scheme that repurposes underused exponent bits to store mask/sign information without separate metadata is a clever systems-level contribution, and the accompanying decode-GEMM kernel is empirically shown to roughly double throughput over cuBLAS on two GPU types.

The empirical evaluation is broad: four MoE model families, nine+ benchmarks (general reasoning, math, code), multiple sparsity levels, and 16 random seeds reported with low variance, supporting the robustness claim of random pairwise grouping.

Extensive ablations are provided (calibration dataset choice, grouping strategy, similarity threshold, saliency metric variants, number of experts merged, combination with quantization, extension to higher sparsity), which is unusually thorough for this type of systems/algorithms paper.
A theoretical (Gaussian-based) argument for element-wise weight similarity is provided and is reasonably well validated empirically on two of the three tested model families.
weaknesses: Several baseline numbers in the main tables (D2, Sub-MoE, STUN) contain missing entries (dashes) for multiple benchmarks and are reported at different, non-matching sparsity ratios (e.g., D2 at 20%/40% vs. PuzzleMoE at 25%/50%), suggesting these numbers were directly copied from the original papers rather than reproduced under an identical evaluation protocol. This undermines the fairness and rigor of the central comparison that drives the paper's main accuracy claims.

The theoretical derivation (Lemma 3.1) assumes independence between expert weight elements, which the authors' own appendix analysis (Table 7) shows is violated for Mixtral-8x7B (correlation 0.26), yet Mixtral is the model used most prominently throughout the main results; this weakens the stated generality of the probabilistic motivation.

The efficient bit-packed inference pipeline is fundamentally restricted to pairwise (2-to-1) merging; higher compression via 3-to-1/4-to-1 merging (Appendix A.8.4/A.8.2) requires abandoning the bit-packing scheme and storing masks explicitly, which reintroduces the exact metadata overhead the paper's core efficiency contribution is designed to eliminate. This limits the practical scope of the 'efficient inference' claim to a narrow regime.

The decode-GEMM kernel and end-to-end throughput experiments are only benchmarked on consumer-grade GPUs (RTX 4090/5090), not on data-center hardware (A100/H100) where large MoE models are actually deployed; it is unclear whether the claimed 1.8x throughput gain and exponent-shift/bit-packing tricks transfer to tensor-core-optimized datacenter kernels or to FP8/other dtypes increasingly used in production.

The method still requires a calibration dataset to compute activation-based saliency scores (contradicting an implicit framing of the method as training/calibration free), and while robustness to calibration data choice is shown for one model, this is not verified across all four evaluated models.

The exponent-shifting trick depends on an empirically narrow exponent range; outlier weights below the cutoff are clipped (rounded up), and while perplexity is reportedly unaffected for the models tested, there is no analysis of how this generalizes to models/layers with heavier-tailed weight distributions or future architectures.

Presentation includes some overreaching claims (e.g., repeated 'first' framing) and the qualitative comparison table (Figure 1b, Low/Medium/High ratings) is subjective and not rigorously justified with quantitative thresholds.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated problem (fine-grained vs. coarse-grained expert merging) and supports the motivation with both a probabilistic analysis (Lemma 3.1) and empirical validation across multiple MoE models (Figure 2, Appendix A.5-A.6), giving the dual-mask design a principled grounding.

The dual-mask merging algorithm (similarity-based + saliency-based) is a clean, training-free, single-pass method that cleverly separates shared vs. specialized weights at the element level, addressing a real limitation of prior coarse-grained expert dropping/merging methods.

The bit-packing scheme that reuses underutilized exponent bits to embed masks/signs without extra metadata storage is a genuinely useful systems-level insight, and the custom decode-GEMM Triton kernel is shown to deliver close to the theoretical 2x speedup over cuBLAS on two different GPUs (Appendix A.1), with end-to-end throughput gains up to 1.8x.

Extensive empirical evaluation: four MoE model families, perplexity plus seven zero-shot reasoning benchmarks, math reasoning (GSM8K, Math-500, AIME), coding (HumanEval), multiple sparsity levels including very high sparsity (66.7%, 75%), and averaging over 16 random seeds to demonstrate robustness to expert grouping choice.

Thorough ablation studies covering calibration dataset choice, grouping strategy (random vs. search), similarity threshold, saliency metric variants, number of experts merged, and compatibility with quantization, which substantially strengthens confidence in the robustness of the design choices.
Compression time analysis shows PuzzleMoE is far cheaper than SVD-based (D2) or exhaustive-search-based (NAEE) baselines, supporting practicality claims.
weaknesses: The theoretical Gaussian-independence assumption underlying Lemma 3.1 is explicitly violated for Mixtral-8x7B (correlation 0.26 in Appendix A.6), one of the main evaluated and best-performing models, which weakens the generality of the stated theoretical justification for exactly the model where the method is showcased most prominently.

The method is fundamentally restricted to pairwise (2-expert) merging to keep the bit-packing scheme tractable; the paper's own appendix (A.8.2, A.8.4) shows that going beyond pairwise merging degrades accuracy and requires abandoning the bit-packing memory savings, so the practical compression ratio achievable while retaining the full efficiency benefits is capped at 50% expert reduction.

Several baseline numbers in the main comparison tables (e.g., D2 and Sub-MoE rows) are incomplete (missing BoolQ/MMLU/average values), which are presumably taken directly from the original papers without being re-run under the same evaluation harness; this makes some head-to-head comparisons less rigorous and harder to verify for fairness.

Throughput and kernel benchmarks are conducted only on consumer RTX4090/5090 GPUs, whereas the deployment motivation in the introduction centers on datacenter-scale needs (e.g., multi-A100 Mixtral deployment); no results are shown on datacenter GPUs (A100/H100) where memory-bandwidth characteristics and tensor-core utilization differ, leaving the practical deployment benefit partially unverified.

The core technical components (magnitude-based similarity merging, Wanda-style activation-weighted saliency, bit-level packing of auxiliary metadata) are individually adaptations of existing ideas from dense-model pruning/quantization literature; the main novelty lies in combining and applying them to MoE expert merging, which is a reasonable but somewhat incremental contribution relative to the strength of the empirical claims ("first" fine-grained element-wise merging method).

The paper does not report explicit peak-memory measurements (only the percentage expert-count reduction and assumed bit savings); an end-to-end memory footprint comparison against baselines (including mask/index overhead for prior fine-grained pruning attempts) would make the memory-saving claims more concrete.

Despite being labeled "task-agnostic," the method still relies on calibration data (128 C4 samples) for saliency computation, and details of how saliency is computed efficiently across many candidate expert pairs for models with large expert counts (e.g., 64 experts in DeepSeek-MoE) are not fully elaborated, leaving some reproducibility questions about the end-to-end compression pipeline cost breakdown beyond the aggregate wall-clock numbers reported.
